problemText: Rudyard Kipling's 1899 poem "The White Man's Burden", urging the United States to take up colonial rule in the Philippines, describes the colonized subjects it addresses as "Your new-caught, sullen peoples," in need of foreign rule. AP World History courses present this poem to students primarily as evidence of —
choices: a formal declaration of war already approved by the United States Congress in 1899
the paternalistic "civilizing mission" argument used to justify empire
an ethnographic survey documenting Filipino political opinion in 1899
a private diplomatic cable never intended for public circulation
hints: Notice the poem addresses American readers, urging them to "take up" a burden — it is a call to action aimed at the colonizing public, not a report from the colonized.
The poem is studied as a primary source OF an imperial ideology (the civilizing mission), not as a neutral or accurate description of the peoples it discusses.

problemText: In the same poem, Kipling instructs colonizers: "To seek another's profit," "And work another's gain." — framing colonial rule as undertaken for the colonized subjects' benefit rather than the colonizer's own. A historian analyzing this claim against the broader economic record of European and American imperialism in this period would most likely note that —
choices: this claim is ideology obscuring the real economic benefits colonizers extracted from colonized regions
the claim is confirmed by the poem's own admission that imperial rule was consistently unprofitable for every colonizing power
the claim reflects a policy formally adopted at the 1919 Paris Peace Conference
the claim describes an arrangement colonized peoples had themselves proposed to colonizing governments
hints: Ask whether a poem written to persuade colonizers to "take up" empire is likely to give an objective account of who actually profited from it.
Rule out any answer treating the poem's self-description as settled historical fact rather than as the ideology it is being studied as.

problemText: In his 1839 letter to Queen Victoria, the Qing commissioner Lin Zexu argues that because opium "is prohibited with the utmost strictness and severity" inside Britain, "you ought not to have the injurious drug transferred to another country". This argument is best characterized as —
choices: a formal declaration of war against Britain over the opium trade
a demand for reparations for damage already caused by the First Opium War
an appeal to Britain's own ban on opium to argue against exporting it abroad
an offer to legalize opium production within China in exchange for lower British tariffs
hints: Lin points to a rule Britain already applies to itself, then asks why that same rule should not extend to what Britain sells abroad.
The letter predates the First Opium War (1839, before fighting began) — rule out any answer describing a response to a war that had not yet happened.

problemText: Lin Zexu also tells Queen Victoria that Chinese exports like tea and rhubarb are "things which your foreign countries could not exist a single day without". Written in 1839, before the First Opium War, this claim most directly reflects which historical situation?
choices: Qing officials' confidence in China's economic leverage over Britain before military defeat forced unequal treaties
a trade agreement already granting British merchants extraterritorial legal rights in Canton
the fact that China had already been formally divided into European colonial spheres of influence by 1839
Britain's total naval and military dominance over the Qing dynasty, already established by 1839
hints: The letter comes BEFORE the First Opium War — China had not yet suffered the military defeats that produced the unequal treaties and extraterritoriality.
China remained a sovereign Qing state throughout this period under informal imperialism — it was never formally colonized the way parts of Africa or India were.

problemText: Article 34 of the 1885 General Act of the Berlin Conference requires that a power claiming new African coastal territory "shall accompany the respective act with a notification thereof, addressed to the other Signatory Powers of the present Act". This clause is best understood as establishing which principle among the fourteen signatory powers (which included the Ottoman Empire) for recognizing a new colonial claim in Africa?
choices: that all fourteen signatory powers, including the Ottoman Empire, had to unanimously approve any new claim before it took effect
that a new claim required the written consent of the African rulers whose territory was being claimed
an outright ban on any signatory power acquiring further African territory after 1885
formal notification to the other European signatory powers, with no requirement of consent from any African government
hints: The clause is addressed to "the other Signatory Powers" — read carefully for who is being notified, and who is conspicuously absent from that requirement.
This is the 'effective occupation' rule: European powers recognized each other's claims among themselves, without African governments party to the agreement.

problemText: A data table of INDIAN indentured emigration only (excluding Chinese indenture and smaller streams to Malaya, the Seychelles, and East Africa) to six British colonies, 1834-1917, reports: "British Mauritius, 453,063; British Guiana, 238,909; Trinidad and Tobago, 147,596; British Jamaica, 36,412; Colony of Natal (South Africa), 152,184; Colony of Fiji, 60,965" — a combined 1,089,129 laborers, of which Mauritius and British Guiana together account for roughly 64 percent. This concentration in Mauritius and British Guiana is best explained by —
choices: those two colonies recruiting laborers exclusively from China rather than India
early, large-scale plantation demand in Indian Ocean and Caribbean colonies after 1833 abolition of slavery
a British colonial policy banning Indian indenture recruitment everywhere except Mauritius and Guiana
these six totals representing the complete worldwide scale of unfree Asian labor migration in this period
hints: This table covers Indian indenture only, to six named destinations — it is not a total for all unfree Asian labor migration worldwide.
Indenture recruitment expanded to replace enslaved plantation labor after Britain abolished slavery in 1833 — think about which sugar colonies needed that labor earliest and at the largest scale.

problemText: The same table of Indian indentured emigration, 1834-1917, notes that "Fiji, where indenture began only in 1879, about 13 percent as many" workers arrived as in Mauritius. Why did Fiji receive markedly fewer Indian indentured laborers than Mauritius over the full 1834-1917 period?
choices: Fiji's colonial government prohibited Indian indenture recruitment until 1917
Mauritius's sugar industry collapsed after 1879 and redirected its remaining laborers to Fiji
Fiji recruited its plantation labor exclusively from China rather than from India
Fiji began recruiting decades after Mauritius, leaving far less cumulative recruiting time
hints: Mauritius began recruiting Indian indentured labor soon after the 1833 abolition of slavery; Fiji's recruitment did not begin until 1879 — a difference of decades.
This table counts only Indian indenture — think in terms of total recruiting TIME available to each colony, not a change in which country workers came from.

problemText: Article 1 of the 1868 Charter Oath, issued by the new Meiji government, states: "A deliberative assembly shall be formed, and all measures decided by public opinion." In the context of Japan's reform program after the fall of the Tokugawa shogunate, this article is best read as —
choices: a declaration abolishing the office of emperor entirely
an announcement that Japan had adopted an exact copy of the British parliamentary system in 1868
a general commitment to consultative, public decision-making, without yet specifying a fixed constitutional structure
the extension of voting rights to all adult subjects regardless of status
hints: The Oath was issued in 1868, over two decades before Japan's actual 1889 constitution — it sets a broad principle, not a detailed institutional design.
Rule out any answer describing a specific, already-completed constitutional system rather than a stated intention.

problemText: Article 5 of the Charter Oath declares: "Wisdom and ability should be sought after in all quarters of the world for the purpose of firmly establishing the foundations of the empire." This article is best read as evidence of which broader pattern in Meiji Japan's reform program?
choices: a rejection of all foreign knowledge in favor of preserving indigenous tradition unchanged
openness to useful outside knowledge as part of a selective, state-directed modernization, not wholesale westernization
a plan for Japan to colonize other Asian states specifically to acquire their technical knowledge
proof that Japan had already abandoned the emperor system by 1868
hints: "Sought after in all quarters of the world" signals openness to outside knowledge, but the article frames this as serving Japan's own foundations, not replacing Japanese institutions wholesale.
Meiji Japan is often misdescribed as simply 'westernizing' — the actual program selectively adapted foreign knowledge within a distinctly Japanese political frame.

problemText: At the Battle of Adwa (1896), Emperor Menelik II's Ethiopian forces decisively defeated an invading Italian army, forcing Italy to formally recognize Ethiopian independence. Historians cite Adwa as the clearest counterexample to which generalization about resistance to imperial expansion, 1750-1900?
choices: that resistance movements which failed to preserve independence, like the Sepoy Rebellion of 1857, had no lasting effect on imperial governance
that European powers only attempted to invade regions that lacked any organized indigenous government
that resistance to imperial expansion never succeeded in preserving a threatened state's formal independence
that resistance to imperial expansion always succeeded whenever it relied on conventional military tactics
hints: Adwa is significant because Ethiopia's victory forced a European power to formally back off — think about which broad claim that single fact disproves.

Most resistance movements in this period, including the Sepoy Rebellion, were eventually suppressed, but 'always failed' overstates a real pattern into a false absolute — Adwa is the clean counterexample.

problemText: The First Opium War (1839-1842) ended with the Treaty of Nanjing, which imposed 'unequal treaty' terms on Qing China, including extraterritoriality — the principle that foreign nationals accused of crimes in China would be tried under their own country's laws rather than Chinese law. Which statement best describes what extraterritoriality meant for Qing sovereignty?
choices: it left Qing China formally sovereign but stripped it of legal jurisdiction over foreign nationals within its own territory
it formally transferred all Qing territory to British colonial administration
it required foreign nationals in China to be tried only under Qing law in every case
it abolished the Qing dynasty and replaced it with a British-appointed government
hints: Extraterritoriality is a legal carve-out, not a formal transfer of territory or government.
Rule out any answer describing full colonization, a reversed legal rule, or the Qing dynasty's abolition — China remained a sovereign Qing state under informal imperialism.

problemText: Unlike much of Africa and South Asia, China was never formally partitioned into European colonies; instead, foreign powers carved out "spheres of influence" — regions of exclusive economic and political privilege — while the Qing dynasty remained nominally sovereign. Which statement best captures why historians classify this arrangement as "informal imperialism" rather than formal colonization?
choices: foreign powers had no meaningful economic or political influence in China at all during this period
the Qing dynasty formally ceded all of its territory to a single foreign power under one comprehensive treaty
spheres of influence gave the Qing dynasty exclusive control over foreign merchants operating within its borders
foreign powers exercised substantial economic and political control without formally replacing Qing sovereignty with direct colonial administration
hints: Informal imperialism means real foreign control without formally replacing the existing government.
Rule out any answer denying real foreign influence, describing a single comprehensive cession, or reversing who controlled whom.

problemText: After Britain abolished slavery in 1833, British colonial planters turned to indentured labor, recruiting workers under contracts binding them to work for a fixed number of years in exchange for passage and wages. Which statement best describes why colonial planters adopted this labor system?
choices: to replace the enslaved plantation labor force that abolition had eliminated
to comply with a new law requiring planters to import laborers only from southern China
to end every form of contracted or bound labor on British Caribbean plantations within a decade
to provide a form of paid vacation labor for British citizens seeking overseas travel
hints: Indenture expanded specifically to fill the labor gap abolition created on plantations.
Rule out any answer requiring exclusively Chinese recruitment, ending all bound labor, or describing indenture as vacation travel — none matches the historical record.

problemText: Historians estimate that Mauritius and British Guiana together received roughly 64 percent of all Indian indentured laborers transported between 1834 and 1917, far more than smaller destinations like Fiji. Beyond Fiji's later 1879 start date, which additional factor most plausibly explains this concentration in Mauritius and British Guiana specifically?
choices: both colonies banned the recruitment of any laborers other than those from India
both had large, well-established sugar plantation economies with an especially urgent labor need immediately after the 1833 abolition of slavery
both colonies were located in the Pacific Ocean, closer to Indian ports than any Caribbean colony
both colonies had no sugar industry and instead recruited indentured labor for mining
hints: Sugar plantations were the primary post-abolition source of labor demand for indenture across British colonies.
Rule out any answer involving a ban on non-Indian labor, incorrect geography, or a non-sugar industry — Mauritius and Guiana were major sugar producers.

problemText: The Berlin Conference's "effective occupation" principle required a European power to notify other signatory powers of a new African territorial claim, but imposed no requirement that African governments consent to or even be informed of that claim. Which conclusion about the imperial "scramble for Africa" does this principle best support?
choices: African governments held equal negotiating status alongside European powers at the Berlin Conference itself
the principle required African governments to formally ratify any new European claim before it could take effect
European powers structured mutual recognition of colonial claims among themselves, treating African political consent as unnecessary
the principle banned any further European territorial claims in Africa after 1885
hints: Notice who the notification requirement is addressed to — other European powers, not African governments.
Rule out any answer granting African governments negotiating status, requiring their ratification, or claiming a post-1885 claims ban — none matches the Berlin Act's actual terms.

problemText: When the British governor demanded that the Asante Empire surrender the Golden Stool — the sacred symbol of Asante royal authority — Yaa Asantewaa, Queen Mother of Ejisu, rallied Asante forces to resist in the War of the Golden Stool (1900). Which statement best describes the outcome and significance of this resistance?
choices: the uprising succeeded in expelling British colonial forces from the entire Gold Coast region for good
the British governor formally withdrew his demand for the Golden Stool right after the uprising's opening skirmish
Yaa Asantewaa's forces were decisively defeated in their very first engagement against regular British colonial troops
the uprising was suppressed and Asante formally annexed, though it stands out for a woman leading the state's major armed resistance
hints: The War of the Golden Stool was ultimately suppressed, but its leadership and scale remain historically significant.
Rule out any answer claiming a full British withdrawal, a withdrawn demand, or no armed engagement — the war was fought and then suppressed.

problemText: The Boxer Uprising (1899-1901) besieged foreign legations in Beijing with eventual Qing court support, but was suppressed by an international Eight-Nation Alliance force, resulting in the Boxer Protocol (1901). Which statement best characterizes this outcome relative to most other resistance movements covered in this topic?
choices: the Boxer Uprising's suppression led to an even harsher round of foreign intervention, imposing a large indemnity and further concessions on China
unlike most suppressed resistance, the Boxer Uprising's suppression brought immediate relief from foreign intervention rather than harsher terms
the Boxer Uprising succeeded in ending every foreign sphere of influence in China for good
the Boxer Uprising was resolved through diplomatic negotiation alone, without any foreign military intervention at all
hints: The Boxer Protocol imposed a large indemnity and further concessions — not relief.
Rule out any answer describing relief from intervention, an end to spheres of influence, or a purely diplomatic resolution — the uprising was suppressed militarily by an international coalition.

problemText: The Zulu Kingdom inflicted a major defeat on British forces at the Battle of Isandlwana (1879) but was ultimately defeated later that same year, while Ethiopia's victory at the Battle of Adwa (1896) preserved its independence for decades afterward. Which factor best explains why Adwa produced a lasting result that Isandlwana did not?
choices: the Zulu Kingdom's warriors carried more modern breech-loading rifles than Ethiopia's army did at the Battle of Adwa
Ethiopia fielded a large, unified army under Menelik II against a small, overextended Italian force, while Britain could reinforce after Isandlwana
Britain formally recognized full Zulu independence immediately after Isandlwana, just as Italy later recognized Ethiopian independence after Adwa
Italy fielded a substantially larger and better-supplied invading army at Adwa than Britain committed during the entire Anglo-Zulu War
hints: Ask what happened AFTER each initial battle — one invading power could reinforce and ultimately prevail; the other could not.
Rule out any answer claiming superior Zulu weaponry, an immediate British recognition of Zulu independence, or a larger Italian force — none matches the historical record.

problemText: The Meiji government issued the Charter Oath in 1868, shortly after the fall of the Tokugawa shogunate. Which of the following best describes the Charter Oath's basic purpose?
choices: to formally abolish the imperial throne and replace it with an elected Meiji parliament
to establish, in 1868, Japan's first detailed and fully drafted written national constitution
to set out broad guiding principles for Japan's new government, favoring consultative rule and openness to outside knowledge
to declare war on Qing China immediately following the Tokugawa shogunate's collapse in 1868
hints: The Charter Oath set broad principles in 1868, well before Japan's detailed 1889 constitution.
Rule out any answer describing abolishing the emperor, a full constitution, or an immediate declaration of war — none describes the Oath's actual content.

problemText: Meiji Japan's reform program selectively adapted foreign knowledge and technology within a framework that preserved and strengthened the emperor's central authority, while Qing China's roughly contemporary Self-Strengthening Movement attempted to adopt foreign technology without comparably restructuring its political institutions. Which conclusion do historians most often draw from contrasting these two reform efforts?
choices: both reform efforts followed the same scope, timing, and top-down political approach to modernization
Qing China's own Self-Strengthening Movement restructured its central government institutions far more thoroughly than Meiji Japan's reforms did
neither Meiji Japan nor Qing China adopted meaningful Western military or industrial technology during this period
Meiji Japan paired technological adoption with political restructuring, explaining its more thorough modernization than Qing's Self-Strengthening effort
hints: The key contrast is technological adoption ALONE (Self-Strengthening) versus technological adoption paired with institutional restructuring (Meiji Japan).
Rule out any answer treating the two efforts as identical, reversing which state restructured institutions more, or denying either adopted foreign technology.

problemText: Historians identify several combined causes of the late-nineteenth-century "New Imperialism": industrial demand for raw materials and new markets, nationalist competition among European powers, the pseudo-moral "civilizing mission" ideology, and military technology advantages such as the Maxim gun and quinine treatment for malaria. Which of these is best classified as a technological, rather than economic or ideological, cause?
choices: the Maxim gun and quinine, giving European forces a decisive military and medical edge in colonial campaigns
the industrial demand for raw materials such as rubber, oil, cotton, and tin ore
the 'civilizing mission' ideology, used to justify colonial rule as a moral obligation
nationalist competition among rival European powers racing to claim territory before others did
hints: Distinguish a technological/medical cause (weapons, disease treatment) from economic (raw materials/markets), ideological ("civilizing mission"), and political (nationalist rivalry) causes.
The Maxim gun and quinine are the technological/medical factor among the four.

problemText: The Berlin Conference (1884-85) brought European powers together to establish rules for dividing African territory among themselves. Which statement best describes a defining feature of this conference?
choices: it was attended by delegates from every major African kingdom and empire, who jointly approved the resulting borders
it drew colonial borders across Africa without African governments' participation, cutting across ethnic and political lines
it formally ended all European colonization of Africa
it was convened specifically to abolish the slave trade throughout the African continent
hints: African governments were not represented at the conference — its participants were entirely European powers.
Rule out any answer claiming African participation, an end to colonization, or a focus on abolishing the slave trade — none describes the conference's actual purpose or attendance.

problemText: Colonial governments in this period often built railroads, telegraph lines, and other infrastructure in their African and Asian territories. Which statement best evaluates the claim that this infrastructure primarily served the interests of colonized populations?
choices: colonial infrastructure was built mainly for the comfort of colonized populations, with almost no economic function for colonizers
colonial governments generally built no rail, port, or telegraph infrastructure anywhere in their African or Asian territories
colonial infrastructure was built mainly to extract raw materials and move them toward colonial ports, not to serve local development
colonial infrastructure investment was split evenly between resource-extraction projects and locally directed community development projects
hints: Ask what a railroad running from an inland resource to a coastal port was actually built to accomplish.
Rule out any answer claiming no infrastructure was built, that it served colonized populations exclusively, or that investment was evenly split — none matches the historical pattern.

problemText: King Leopold II ran the Congo Free State as his own personal colonial possession from 1885 to 1908, extracting rubber through a forced-labor system that killed an estimated several million Congolese, before international pressure forced him to cede the territory to the Belgian government. Which feature makes the Congo Free State a distinctive, rather than typical, case within the broader history of this period's imperialism?
choices: it was the only colonial territory anywhere in Africa where forced labor of any kind was ever documented
it was the only nineteenth-century case in which international public pressure ever forced a colonial power to change policy
Leopold II personally governed the territory in close, continuous cooperation with an elected Belgian parliament from day one
the territory was held as one monarch's personal possession rather than a state-administered colony, removing limited government oversight
hints: The Congo Free State's defining feature was personal royal ownership, distinct from state-administered colonies elsewhere.

Rule out any answer claiming forced labor was unique to the Congo, that international pressure never mattered elsewhere, or that Leopold governed through an elected parliament from the start — none matches the historical record.
